Narito ang gámit nila. (a) Ginagamit ang pahilis para markahán ang pantig na may diin. Maaari ito sa mga salitáng binibigkas nang malumay: áhu ‘áso’; dúngu ‘sikmura’; lábuk ‘buhok’; úu ‘ulo’. Ginagamit din ito para sa mga salitang binibigkas nang mabilis: buyá ‘bigas’; buktút ‘buntis’; maí ‘mais’; tuúk ‘tainga’; mangán ‘kain’. (b) Ginagamit ang paiwa para markahán ang salitáng nagtatapos sa impit na tunog na binibigkas nang malumì: kakà ‘ate/kuya’; dirà ‘mutà’; gawù ‘tuyong buho na ginagamit sa apoy’. (c) Ginagamit ang pakupya para markahán ang salitáng may impit na tunog at diin sa hulíng pantig: kalupî ‘bayong’; hirâ ‘karne/sira’. new_statements.translation: Three diacritics may be used in Magbukun: acute ( ´ ), grave ( ` ) and circumflex ( ˆ ). They are to be used on words that are spelled alike but differ in meaning. ... (a) The acute is used to mark the syllable that carries the stress. It can be used on words pronounced malumay [penultimate stress]: áhu 'dog', dúngu 'stomach', lábuk 'hair', úu 'head'. It is also used for words pronounced mabilis [final stress]: buyá 'husked rice', buktút 'pregnant', maí 'corn', tuúk 'ear', mangán 'eat'. ... (c) The circumflex is used to mark a word that has a [final] glottal stop and stress on the last syllable: kalupî 'palm-leaf bag', hirâ 'meat / broken'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on either the penultimate or the final syllable and is a lexical property of the word (Filipino-style malumay = penult vs mabilis = final classes); it is not predictable from spelling, so the orthography marks it with an acute (or, combined with a final glottal stop, a circumflex) where homographs must be distinguished. No default position is stated.
new_statements.exceptions: None; diacritics are prescribed only 'for words spelled alike but different in meaning', implying stress is otherwise left unmarked. Grave/circumflex additionally encode a word-final glottal stop (malumì = penult stress + final glottal; maragsâ-type = final stress + final glottal).
new_statements.domain_note: Orthography guide: statements concern citation forms of single words (basic vocabulary list pp. 35 ff. is printed with acute accents on many entries, e.g. abágat, abáya, kaanakán, labíng pitú, providing per-word stress data). Not an acoustic or phonological analysis; the instrumental/phonological treatment is Cruz & Piedad 2022 (not retrieved).
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes 'Ayta Magbukun' (= Bataan Ayta, Magbikin/Magbeken, Mariveleño; Glottolog bata1297, ISO 639-3 ayt), produced with the Ayta Magbukun community (Bangkal, Abucay, Bataan is named), DepEd Schools Division of Bataan and SIL Philippines; published by the Komisyon sa Wikang Filipino. Same languoid as the target; no sub-dialect specified. The 1974 Malicsi thesis on 'Halitaq Baytan (a Sambal Aeta dialect)' is probably also this language ('speech of Bataan') but that identification is unverified.

sources.note: Section 5 'Taw Tuldik / Mga Tuldik' (PDF p.17 = printed pp.32-33): three diacritics; acute marks the syllable bearing stress (diin), used both for words pronounced malumay (penultimate stress: áhu 'dog', dúngu, lábuk, úu) and mabilis (final stress: buyá 'rice', buktút, maí, tuúk, mangán); grave = final glottal stop pronounced malumì (kakà, dirà, gawù); circumflex = final glottal stop plus final-syllable stress (kalupî, hirâ); diacritics are to be written on words spelled alike but differing in meaning. Section 2 'Pantig' gives syllable types V, CV, VC, CVC; no statement of a default stress po…
